hints: Look carefully at Fig. 1.1 - where are the dark vascular tissues located, at the edge in a ring or in the centre, and what fills the large central area?
walkthrough:
Recall the Stem Versus Root Plan**
Think of a young dicotyledonous stem like sunflower as a tube with a ring of separate vascular bundles near the outside and a large ground tissue centre called the pith. A root has its xylem and phloem together in a small central stele, not a ring at the edge.

Apply to Fig. 1.1**
Here you can see discrete bundles (B) arranged in a ring toward the outside and a large area of pale parenchyma cells (A) filling the centre. That matches a stem, so state stem and give the position of bundles and central pith as your reason.
Final answer: Stem, because vascular bundles are at the edge / in a ring with pith / parenchyma in the centre, not in the centre as in a root.

hints: Cell A is in the central pith - it is a large, thin-walled parenchyma cell with a big vacuole. What happens when a plant cell takes up lots of water into its vacuole?
Link that turgid, water-filled property to two jobs a bulky central tissue can do - holding the stem firm and acting as a reservoir.
walkthrough:
Identify the Tissue**
Cell A is parenchyma of the pith and cortex. It has thin cellulose walls, a large central vacuole, and is alive. It is a packing tissue that fills space.

Link Vacuole to Support and Storage**
When water enters by osmosis the vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the wall, making the cell turgid. Masses of turgid parenchyma press on each other to give hydrostatic support to the young stem. The same large vacuole and cytoplasm can store water, starch, sugars and ions, so suggest support with reason of turgidity and storage with reason of vacuole content.
Final answer: Parenchyma for hydrostatic support as cells become turgid when vacuoles fill with water; also for storage of water / starch / sugars / packing.

hints: Structure B is one of the discrete units in the ring that contains both xylem and phloem together - what is the standard name for this combined transport unit in a stem?
walkthrough:
Recognise the Combined Structure**
In a stem, xylem for water transport and phloem for assimilate transport are grouped side by side with strengthening fibres into one unit repeated around the stem. That unit is called a vascular bundle.

hints: Remember $1000 \mu m = 1 mm$. To go from a smaller unit ($\mu m$) to a larger unit (mm), do you need to multiply or divide by 1000?
walkthrough:
Convert Micrometers to Millimetres**
Use $1 mm = 1000 \mu m$. So divide by 1000: $650 \div 1000 = 0.65$. The actual length of structure B is $0.65$ mm.

hints: Start by thinking about life status - one of these conducting elements is dead and hollow at maturity to allow free flow, while the other stays alive but with reduced contents. Which is which?
Next compare the walls and the ends - think about lignin and pits versus sieve plates and plasmodesmata for side-to-side and end-to-end movement.
For your third point, focus on what is missing or present inside: cytoplasm, organelles, nucleus and how the end walls are either completely open or perforated.
walkthrough:
Picture the Xylem Vessel as a Dead Pipe**
A mature xylem vessel element is dead. It has lost its cytoplasm, nucleus and organelles to leave a hollow tube with no resistance to water flow. Its walls are thickened and impregnated with lignin for strength and waterproofing, with pits in the side walls for lateral water movement.

Picture the Sieve Tube as a Living Channel**
A phloem sieve tube element is alive but highly modified. It keeps a thin layer of cytoplasm with few organelles and no nucleus, and its end walls remain as sieve plates with pores. Plasmodesmata connect adjacent elements to allow flow of sucrose solution.

Outline Three Clear Differences**
Compare like with like: 1. contents - xylem empty / no cytoplasm, phloem has cytoplasm. 2. walls - xylem lignified and thicker, phloem not lignified and thinner. 3. ends - xylem no end walls / open, phloem has sieve plates; xylem has pits and no plasmodesmata, phloem has plasmodesmata. Any three such paired differences gain full credit.

Final answer: Xylem vessel element has no cytoplasm / is hollow with no contents / no organelles; walls lignified and thick; no end walls with pits in side walls and no plasmodesmata. Phloem sieve tube element retains some cytoplasm, has sieve plates in end walls and plasmodesmata, is not lignified with thinner walls.
